candidate.answerReason: Sums, differences, and products of even integers are even. Division can give 1 and is undefined for a zero divisor; the mean of 0 and 2 is 1. Thus only operations 1, 2, and 3 always give elements of S.

methods.label: Prove the successful cases and give counterexamples
methods.explanation:
An operation qualifies only if every pair of elements gives a defined result in \(S\). Write arbitrary elements of \(S\) as \(2u\) and \(2v\), where \(u\) and \(v\) are integers, including possibly zero or negative integers. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
2u+2v&=2(u+v),\\
2u-2v&=2(u-v),\\
(2u)(2v)&=2(2uv).
\end{aligned}
\]
Each result is twice an integer, so addition, subtraction, and multiplication always give elements of \(S\).

One counterexample is enough to rule out an operation that must work for every pair. Division fails because \(2/2=1\notin S\); division by zero is also undefined. Finding the mean fails because
\[
\frac{0+2}{2}=1\notin S.
\]
Thus exactly operations \(\boxed{1,2,3}\) qualify, choice \(\text{D}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses the representation of even integers as multiples of two, elementary arithmetic, and counterexamples.
